A 14-month-old Alexandria girl
was hanged accidentally last night
by a Venetian blind cord dangling
beside her crib.


Alexandria police said the body
Iof Rebecca Anne Walter was
found by her mother. Mrs. Flora
M. Walter. about 7:10 pm. The
cord was entwined around the
baby's neck and police said she
apparently had fallen forward in
the crib while playing with the
cord.


Mrs. Walter told police she had
Iput her daughter in the crib 10
minutes earlier and had gone into
an adjoining room but heard no
outcry.


The Alexandria Rescue Squad
tried to revive Rebecca Anne with
oxygen. but was pronounced dead
on arrival at Alexandria Hospital.


Rebecca Anne's father, Oakley
IS. Walter. is employed at the Navy
Department. The Walters live at
1870 Prince street, Alexandria.
Rebecca Anne was their only
child.

Planners of the growing Alexandria of today
are showing commendable determination to pre-
serve the Alexandria of yesterday-the old vii
lage of Revolutionary and pre-Revolutionary
times The Alexandria Planning Commission,
with proper respect for the citys many historical
associations, has recommended that the master
zoning plan for the city provide safeguards for
the Colonial appearance of what Alexandrians
fondly call the "old town"


Much of the "old town" remains today re-
markably as it was in the days when George
Washington, George Mason and others enjoyed
its hospitality. Many of the venerable homes
have been restored by private owners, proud of
the antiquity which sets these quaint properties
apart from the homes and apartments in
Alexandrias more modern residential districts.
Others, like the famous Ramsay House, have been
saved by community action. Leading in the
movement to protect the Older sections of the
city from commercial encroachment have been
such organizations as the Old Town Civic Asso-
citation and the Alexandria Association for the
Preservation of the Citys Antiquities

Locust blossoms were falling like

They carpeted the walks and the
grass, and spread their greenish- white

This was sort of new snow, the
wind blowing the little blossoms gently
into heaps here and there, as they
congregated at steps and house walls.


Many bees buzzed in the trees, seek
ing the honey dew. Some years they
make the trees loud with their hum
ming.


This year there were not enough bees
to make noise, but the movement in
among the leaves was perceptible.


Locust trees have many faults, in
cluding shallow roots and much dirt.
but the fall of the tiny flowers is one
of their good points.


Despite the drifts on the walks, there
seemed as many blossoms aloft as ever.


Such is natures profusion.


It is said that 20 million eggs are
! laid to produce one cod.


No one can compute the number OF
locust blossoms to have one tree.


Birds liked to eat the blossoms.


Sparrows deserted the feeding station
back by the yard and sought eagerly
the mounds of blossoms by the front
steps.

PHILADELPHIA Dec. 31.-Four times
the Appalachians from Maine through
the Carolinas have been lifted out of
the sea into mountain ranges as high
as the present Himalayas


The present mountains, the loftiest
OF which is only little more than a
mile high, are the worn-down remains
OF such range which was born about
200,000,000 years ago.


The picture, resulting from determi-
nation OF the ages of Appalachian rocks
from the decay of such radioactive min
erals as uranium and thorium, was
presented to the American Association
for the Advancement of Science here
today by John Rodgers, assistant pro-
fessor Of geology at Yale


The first great Appalachian range,
Mr.. Rodgers said, appeared roughly
800,000,000 years ago. At that time
this was a lifeless planet, at least SO
far as any living things which have
left any traces are concerned. The
land surface, at least, must have been
as barren as Mars.


Crests Were Eaten Away.


But rain fell, frosts cracked rocks
and great winds swept over peaks prob
ably as high as the present. Mount
Everest. Over many, many millions
OF years the great crests were eaten
away and washed into the ancient
ocean which had very roughly the po-
sition Of the present Atlantic North
ern waters rushed into the trough thus
created.


The second Appalachians, the radio
active determinations show, were up-
lifted about 600 ZOO, 900 years ago. This
was just before the dawn of the Cam
brian geological era when life's earliest
traces are found in rocks. There still
are fragments Of these mountains, par
ticularly in the Adirondacks. where COL
lections Of Cambrian fossils have been
made.


The second Himalaya-like range
suffered the same fate as the first and
was succeeded. about 350,000,000 years
ago. by another of roughly the same
proportions. BY this time, the earth
had been covered with vegetation. It
was just at the start of the carboniferous
age when the great coal deposits were
laid down from the great forests of
tree ferns. In these forests were ex-
tremely primitive back-boned animals,
and the first fish were in the seas.


Earth Extremely Active.


Throughout most of this period, it
appears, the face Of the globe was ex-
tremely active and the mountains were
short-lived. In the course of about a
hundred million years they had been
washed away and another range raised
up along essentially the same line.


Then, about 100000 years later,
there were great earth commissions
which raised them a little higher. It is
the worn-down remains of these which
constitute the present Appalachians.
The process of erosion still is going on,
but not very violently, and the range
probably still has millions of years of
life.


Fragments of all these ranges, how
ever. still exist. They successfully
resisted the erosion processes and prob
ably remained for millions Of years as
underwater mountains before they were
uplifted again. The successive ranges
have been formed Of rocks created out
of sediments washed into the sea.


The present scenery Mr.. Rodgers
said, results from the wearing away
process which has lowered the areas
of relatively weak rocks to make valleys
and low hills and has left the areas of
stronger rocks, like granite, standing
up as the present-day mountains"


Many Cross Checks Made.


This picture rests, he explained. on
about so accurate determinations of the
age OF radioactive rocks. The process is
slow and tedious, but three samples have
been checked and double-checked and
can be used as standards for the others.
One Of these is mineral obtained near
Middletown, Conn, which was formed
during the mountain building episode of
260 million years ago. The other two
are minerals from Westchester County,
New York. which we're formed approxi-
mately $50 million years ago.


OF the other reliable determinations.
about Is, all from New England, agree
with the Middletown material. About
20, from New England and the Caro-
linas. agree with the Westchester min
erals In being about $50 million years
old. The other reliable determinations
are on older rocks, scattered from North
Carolina to Maine, and give ages of
either approximately 600 million or 800
million years.

SINGAPORE, Jan. 20.-Com-
munist financed importers in
Hong Kong have been buying
Malayan rubber in the Singapore
market at the rate of 1000 tons
a day during the past week for
reshipment to Communist China,
reliable rubber trade sources said
today.


The identity of these Red firms
will not be revealed by any local
rubber dealers, however.


Although it is believed Red
Chinese are dealing mainly with
local Chinese rubber firms, it is
possible that some European firms
may be filing some Communist
orders, these sources said.


Surrounded by Secrecy.


Considerable secrecy surrounds
the purchasing. Orders tele-
graphed from Hong Kong are
placed with Singapore exporters.
Brokers for Singapore buyers are
not told for whom the rubber is
intended.


They go around the market
buying from sellers who also do
not know the real buyer.


Hong Kong stepped into the
rubber trade picture last June
when that British colony, which
imported about 800 tons of rub
ber monthly for its own require
ments, suddenly increased orders
to $500 tons a month.
Russia Not Blamed.
Rubber trade sources say Rus
sia is not behind the Hong Kong
rubber rush but Chinese Reds
certainly are.


They also say that Soviet Rus
sia may be buying Malayan rub
ber through London and New
York to divert attention from
here.
Russia imported 68,058 tons of
rubber last year, mainly through
her Black Sea ports. Rubber men
think this amount is far below
the needs of country preparing
for war.

NEW YORK. Nov. 15.-Fire,
fog and bomb scare plagued New
York City commuters today, max

fusion of the morning rush hour.


Developments piled up quickly
to slow the work. bound millions
heading for Offices, stores and
factories.


First, fog settled down on the
New York harbor. delaying Staten
1sland-to-Manhattan ferry boats
as much as half an hour.


Then a fire blazed in a truck
in, the Holland Tunnel, major link
between New York and New Jersey
and the west. It has a capacity
OF $4,000 vehicles a day and most
always is jammed.


Bomb Report Given.


Adding to today's confusion,
some one called police to say a
bomb had been placed in Grand
Central Terminal. Several ramp
areas were closed to the public
while thousands poured through
the building.


The threat was believed a hoax,
Nevertheless, thorough search
was begun.


While all this was going on
long suffering users of the Long
Island Railroad were delayed five
to Is minutes while trainmen in
serted new schedules in their time
. tables and compared new train
times effective today.


Truck Burns in Tunnel.


Holland Tunnel police said the
truck caught fire about $50 feet
inside the Jersey entrance. They
said it carried cartons of empty
glass containers.


New York City firemen put the
blaze out quickly, but the south
tunnel was filled with smoke. All
New York-bound traffic was rout-
ed over one lane of the north tun-
mel. which normally carries two
lanes of traffic westbound from
New York.


The port of New York authority,
which operates the tunnel, said
the south tube would be reopened
before noon.

Reds.

singled and Solly Hemus then

ski fell down and threw past
first base for an error, both run
ners advanced.

The lengthy and popularity mis-
named "tidelands" oil controversy was
famed into fame again last week
when the House approved a bill by
Representative Walter, Democrat, OF
PENNSYLVANIA which, if enacted into
law, will overturn three recent Su-
preme Court decisions and take ire
mendous oil reserves from Federal
control.


Since 1887, the word "tidelandS"
has cropped up with increasing fire.
quency, and if the layman is slightly
confused by the arguments, it's small
wonder. For the catchword tide
lands" is in itself a miSnomer. Geo.
graphically, the word applies to the
land lying between the high tide and
low tide marks Of any coastal area.
These strips average 100 to 200 yards
in width and are not involved in the
current dispute, since they are legally
recognized as the property OF the
States they adjoin.


With oil and it's financial and ma
tional defense potentialities involved,
the current argument begins where
the tidelands strips end. It covers
the off-shore ocean bottom known as
the continental shelf of the United
States-commonly defined as the area
extending from the shoreline to any
point where the ocean depth exceeds
600 feet


Apart from national defense re-
quirementS, the Federal Government
isn't interested in what happens on
the ocean surface above this shelf.
The States rights to control fishing,
crime and other matters within the
"three-mile limit" of coastal waters
is recognized legally, but the Govern
ment contends that it owns the land
beneath the ocean under international
law.


Whose OiIfieIds?


Most coastal States have no quar-
rel on this question. But for Cali
fornia, Texas and Louisiana, control
of these submerged off-shore lands
involves millions of dollars from the
rich oil deposits in the ocean bed.
About so years ago, oil was discov-
cred off the California coast, and
until 1887, the United States Gov
eminent was content to let the State
issue leases to private interests for
exploitation. AS recently as 1888, the
Interior Department refused to issue
Federal permits for private prospect
ing in the area. contending that it
was State controlled matter.


But the Navy for years has pressed
for huge Federally owned oil reserves
and in 1887, the Interior Department
reversed it's position and decided that
the off-shore oil fields were Govern
ment property.


The States involved reacted quickly.
and Louisiana arbitrarily proclaimed
ownership of all off-shore land ex-
tending 81 miles into the Gulf of
Mexico Texas, acting under its con-
stitution and the terms of its ad-
mittance into the Union, claimed
rights to "three-league" Q012
niles area off shore. In 1941, the
Lone Star State extended this claim
to q miles, and then in 1947 an
nounced ownership Of the entire con-
tinental shelf of its shore. California
stuck to the three-mile limit.

The Senate has approved classified pay
raise bill that is better than the pending House
measure in two outstanding respects First, the
Senate bill would preserve the general balance
OF the Federal pay structure as worked out in
the recent Redistribution Act. Second the
Senate bill would assure WaShington's teachers
policemen and f1remen of co-equal treatment
with classified workers


The Senate was inconsistent however in
refusing to place $400 floor under raises for
classified employees Such anlinimum raise was
voted last week for postal workers, along with
general raise of 8.8 per cent If any floor is
to be set for one group of Government employees
it should apply to all. However the Civil Service
Commission is against the floor idea on the
reasonable ground that it would favor one class
of employees with much larger percentage raise
than other classes, thereby upsetting the care
fully devised relation between pay groups in
the Federal service. The pay bill proposed by
the House Civil Service Committee would further
throw things out of kter by giving all groups
fiat $400 raise. Since this would mean steadily
diminishing percentage raises from bottom to
top, the commission has urged plan similar to
that adopted by the Senate.


Inclusion of local teachers, firemen and
policemen in the Senate bill is sensible precau-
tion against possible discrimination. The House
bill originally had like provision, but it was
stricken because the House District Committee
wanted to sponsor separate legislation for these
employees. But separate legislation runs the risk
of getting lost in the shuttle during the closing
days of the session. The House would relieve
the minds of the District educational and pro-
tective groups if it dropped the separate bill
plan in favor of the Senate omnibus pay measure

CALGARY, Alberta. Oct. 49,
Princess Elizabeth and her hus-
band today entered the carefree
roistering atmosphere of Calgary
at stampede time-a special stam-
pede just for them.


Their schedule here listed a
brief stop at city hall, and then
the wraps were off. A chuckwagon
luncheon (sowbelly and beef stew
and a baby stampede complete
with bucking broncs, chuck wagon
races, wild steers and scads of real,
live Indians were on the f1ve-hour
program.


The only hitch was the weather.
The forecast was for the same cold
and snow furries that marred the
couples visit to Regina yesterday
The days high was expected to be
rs.


But if Saskatchewan's weather
was cold yesterday, the welcome
for Princess Elizabeth and Philip
certainly was not. Thousands
stood for hours in a biting north
west wind for the chance to see
the royal visitors. Some children
were so chilled they had to be
given first aid.


Because of the cold, the princess
wore for the first time since her
arrival at Montreal the full-length
mink coat which was her wedding
present from the Canadian people.
She kept it tightly buttoned
through the outdoor part of her
Regina visit, smuggling comfort
ably in the high, turned-up collar.

The French Army reported today
it had crushed new, two-pronged
Wet Mini offensive to link Com
munist forces in Central Indo-
China with those near the Chinese
border.


The drives were the biggest by
the Wet Mini since last May.
Both attacks were launched Mon
day morning.


The strongest came at Hoa
Binh, a vital highway center 40
miles southwest of Hanoi. The
town was the last Communicated
road link between north and south
until French and Allied Wet
Namese forces drove the Reds out
of it month ago.


Elements of two Wet Mimi di-
visions attacked along the Black
River, the French said, with Com
munist troops infiltrating French
lines, then regrouping for attacks
from the rear. Aerial napalm
bombs helped halt the attack and
a French-Viet Namese counter
offensive drove the Reds westward
into the hills.


The second attack was at Plat
Diem, rs miles southwest of
Hanoi. 1t was aimed at getting a
foothold on the fringe of the Red
River delta. This attack also was
beaten off.


Fighting lasted for 48 hours and
the French estimated more than
1000 rebels were killed in the Hoa
Binh fighting along the Black
River. The French reported their
own losses were only is and said
strong Notifications on the Black
River protected them from heavy
casualties.

/. The earthquake shook Wash

CAIRO, Egypt. Oct. 11.-Shout-
ing Egyptians. demanding the
custer of British troops from
Egypt. demonstrated against Brit
ain today for the second successive
day. but this time there was no
violence.


Heavy police escorts kept order
as thousands paraded through
Mustafa Kamel Square, then
moved on to the larger Ibrahim
Pasha Square to hear speakers
shout:


Down with Britain. We want
the British to get out of our
country"


Leading the crowd. Sudanese
students at two Cairo universities
cried, Down with foreign domi-
nation-we want one King, one
crown, one Nile"


After streaming past the palace
and cheering King Farouk, the
crowds dispersed without incident.


Anti-foreign mobs yesterday
smashed British and French busi-
ness offices. hurled bottles looted
from American soft-drink distrib-
utors' trucks, and set fires.


Back British Custer.


The demonstrations are the
product of violent public support
for the plan of Prime Minister
Mustapha Nahas el Pasha to oust
British troops from the Suez
Canal zone and take full control
|of the jointly ruled Anglo -Egyp-
tian Sudan.


Shopkeepers hastily lowered
steel shutters as the crowds
gathered today.


The huge crowd streamed to-
ward Mustafa Kamel Square to
hear speeches delivered from near
the statue of Mustafa Kamel, an
CByPlldu nero.


Kamel led the Nationalist Party
until his death in 1908. and spear
headed fight for Egyptian in
dependence from the British who
had obtained protectorate over
the country.


Meanwhile. the youth committee
of Nahas Pasha's ruling Wafdist
Party appealed for calm and
condemned yesterdays rioting
against foreign business as a
rash action"


But the Wafdist youths strongly
supported the Prime Minister'S
move to break the 1886 Anglo
Egyptian alliance and the 1899
agreement establishing joint rule
over the cotton-growing Sudan
which abuts Egypt on the south.


United Behind Pasha.


All classes and all parties con-
tinued to back the strong Nation
alist stand taken by Nahas Pasha.


A cheering meeting of univer-
sity students passed a resolution
saying they are ready to be
soldiers at the command of the
government in its struggle against
Imperialism"


Cairo newspapers said the gov
ernment is studying the possibility
OF negotiating non-aggression
pacts with Russia, the , United
States and France-big powers
which, unlike Britain. have no
troops in Egypt.


The 1896 pact gives Britain the
right to keep 10000 troops and
400-plane air force on Egyptian
soil to guard the Suez Canal.


Concerned about the state of
Middle Eastern defenses, the
North Atlantic Treaty Organiza-
ton is planning a multi-nation
Middle East Defense Command
TO defend the area, including the
Suez Canal. Nahas Pasha's
abrupt action has thrown this
proposal in jeopardy.


Study New Alliances.


Local papers said Foreign Min
lister Mohamed Salah ell Din
Pasha mentioned the possibility of
new alliances when he appeared
before a Chamber of Deputies
committee studying bills to carry
out Nahas Pasha's denunciation
Of the pacts with Britain.

oust the British Governor General

choice. The governor generals

News of the coca plant, or shrub,

tests with it. Some of them re-

I'VE have seen people who chewed

eyes become Sunken."


p Those words of warning had only

laboratories, and at length way

the leaves. This was done by
chemist named Albert Niemann
and he called the product cocaine" ;"


Cat this point let me note that
the coca shrub is entirely different
from the cacao tree which provides
the world with cocoa.)


When cocaine came to be known,
there was widespread excitement.
The story spread that it would cure

BERLIN, Sept. 8.-Soviet East

them confiscating each others
autos and trucks in hectic 30
hour tit-for- tat.


But the tax which started it all
remained. This was the toll which
the East German Communists are
exacting from West Berlin and
West German vehicles which
travel through the Russian occu-
patton zone on Berlin's lifeline to
the West.


The war within the city ended
when the West promised to seize
no more Soviet sector vehicles and
pulled back the police reinforce
mentS it had rushed to the sec
tor borders during the tax con-
troverSy.


Thereupon the East Berlin Com
munists began releasing several
hundred West Berlin cars and
trucks they had impounded yes
terday afternoon, last night and
this morning. They promised to
collect no toll on these vehicles
because the West promised to re-
pay what its police had taken.


Western police stopped seizing
Eastern vehicles shortly after
noon yesterday. The Western
action lasted only Az hours and
was conducted by a borough
Mayor without authorization from
the city government. He was
reprimanded by the government
for his one-man reprisal action,
but by that time the Communists
had instituted their counter
reprisal and the war was on again


Meanwhile. it was up to the
Russians to decide whether the
original cause of all this ruckus
could be resolved. That was the
road tax imposed on West Berlin
and West German vehicles which
carry Berlin's lifeline traffic with
the West through the surrounding
Russian occupation zone.

SEOUL, Korea, Dec. Clouds
and fog restricted air activity to-
day and brought the Korean war
to a virtual halt.


The United States 5th Air Force
issued no noon summary, indi-
eating there had been no major
action. The weatherman said
none was possible unless the skies
cleared.


Doughboys in mist-draped hills
across the front held their fire as
the twilight war continued.


A half dozen patrols poked out
across the hill country west of
Yonchon, holding up and calling
for artillery support at the first
sign of Reds.


Five Above Zero in West.


West of the Punchbowl, on the
eastern front. one Red probing
force of about two platoons was
hurled back after a brief skirmish


Temperatures ranged from 5
degrees above zero in the east to
40 above in the west.


Tuesday night seven BIS
Superforts dropped 10 tons OF
bombs on Red troops behind the
Communist front lines. -Four
other B-29s attacked Red Korean
rail yards.


The bombers encountered anti
aircraft fire. but none was dam
aged, the Far East Air Forces said.


Night-f1ying medium bombers
attacked Red highway traffic and
reported more than so vehicles
! destroyed. Other bombers hit rail
targets.


Two MICS Probably Destroyed.


American F-S6 Sabre jet pilots
reported two Russian-made MIG
Is jets probably were destroyed
and two others damaged Thurs
day as FEAT planes mounted 945
sorties. The Air Force said all
Sabre jets returned safely.

munist rail and highway net
works.

a convoy of 40 trucks loading
supplies near Kang Dong and re-
ported destruction of all the
trucks and IS per cent Of the
supplies.


Naval Guns Hammer Coasts.


There was no letup Tuesday in
the Allied naval war against the
Reds. Carrier-based planes and
naval artillery hammered Com
munist targets on both the east
and west coasts.


Naval headquarters in Tokyo
said, the carrier Valley Forge re-
joined Task Force II for her third
tour in Korean waters. That was
1T months and eight days after
she launched the first offensive
mission by an American carrier in
the Korean war July 3, 1850.


In Korea's southern provinces,
where Republic of Korea forces
have been hunting Red guerrillas
and bandits, action was tapering
off. An 9th Army spokesman said
the mopping up in the Mount
Chiri area was finished ito all
intents and purposes.

erS said that 3,739 trees were

while replacements for trees killed
by gas, disease, traffic, vandalism,
storm damage and widening of
driveways and streets accounted
for the rest, it was said.

30,014 trees of low limbs and dead
and dangerous limbs.

combat perennial pests such as
tent caterpillars, elm leaf, elm
bark and japanese beetles. Special
attention went to the $4,000 elm
trees.

ing program for locating elm trees
showing symptoms of the Dutch
elm disease. All elms were ex-I
amined periodically. When signs
of infection appeared, specimens
were sent for laboratory inspec-
tion.


Dead and dying elms found to
have the disease were removed
and burned.

japanese beetles was undertaken
in the spring, the division said.

some areas with the milky spore
disease to prevent metamorphose
of grubs into beetles.


The division called results of

evidenced by the decrease of
beetles during the past summer"

Residents Of Belle Haven, Va,
have won ownership of the sewer
system in their subdivision, after
"a controversy that dates back to
1943.


Federal Judge A. s. Barksdale
decided the case last week and has
entered an order in Alexandria
District Court in favor of the Belle
Haven residents.


His opinion holds that the Gov
ernment was not entitled to take
over the Belle Haven sewers at
the time it installed the Holmes
Run sewer system in Fairfax
County about 10 years ago.


System Since Sold.


The Government. has claimed it
was permitted to condemn the
Belle Haven sewers by the Lanham
Act. but Judge Barkdale's decision
finds that was not the type of
condemnation contemplated under
the Lanham Act. Since the con-
demnation, the Government has
sold the entire system to Fairfax
County.


One Of the major issues involv-
ed was over the monthly sewer
service charges. The Belle Haven
residents claimed that they owned
the sewer system, and their
monthly sewer service rates should
not cover any amortization.


The county bought the Holmes
Run sewer from the Government
for $500,000, and part of the sew
'er service charges throughout
Sanitary District No. go to re-
tire bonds issued for that purpose.
The bond issue totaling SO million
also covers construction of a sew
age disposal plant and extension
of sewer lines throughout the dis
trict.


Monthly Charge Cut.


While the Government owned
the Holmes Run sewer system, the
monthly service charge was So.
The county has reduced the
charge to $3.50 since acquiring the
system several years ago.


James j. Corbalis. jr., county
sanitary engineer, said he would
meet with Government attorneys
to study the decision. He said
Belle Haven sewer fees have not
been collected during the contro-
versy. There are about $50 resi-
dents affected.


The Belle Haven system was in
stalled before the Holmes Run
trunk sewer, but was connected up
with the Federal system about 10
years ago.

Two teen-age District youths

got in of her own accord.

she submitted willingly.


After the incident, she went to
a nearby house, where residents
summoned her mother.


After questioning the girl and
the boys, who were picked up
after she gave police their names,
the assault and battery charges
were placed when the mother de-
cided she did not want to press
more serious charges.

Looking for new dish that
combines these old standbys,
potatoes and onions? Well. try
this Mashed Potato and Onion
Fluff:


Chop cups boiled onions fine
and add them to 2 cups Of mashed
potatoes. Beat in "a cup Of rich
milk or cream, together with the
yolks of 2 eggs. Season with
salt and some chopped parsley.
Beat all until very light end
fluffy.


Beat up the egg whites until
they are stiff and fold them into
the potato and onion mixture.
Turn into a creased casserole and
bake in a rather slow oven for
about " hour; then increase the
heat for S minutes so that the
potatoes will brown nicely on top.

torney Nicholas Berkos.


The Federal grand jury began

3-Day Riots in July.


The sporadic riots lasted nearly

The disorder stemmed from ef-

family into the all-white suburb.


The indictment charged the
defendants conspired to deprive
Mr.. Clark of his constitutional

rights statutes.

ordered In September by Attorney
General McGrath.


The Cook County grand jury in
dicted Konovsky and five other
persons, but the indictments
against the other five later were
thrown out in court.

ing part in the disorders brought
criticism from Chicago civic
|groupS and individuals.

mer owner of the apartment

sented Mrs. De Rose; Charles

slowly.

gary is controlled by the Com

the Austrian border. With her
maid and Oliver Lantos, a noted
Hungarian radio singer, she left
Budapest February 20 for her
scheduled appearance and then
made a nighttime dash across
the border into Austria.

neglect sometimes ending in discovery that esti-
mates of cost had been exceeded Supplemental

shese added costs, unbalancing budgets which
mad not been designed to meet the extra pay
ments. In this connection the report commented
mat supplemental appropriations were numer-
GUS and rather large in amount" and that in some
instances definite obligations or commitments
were made before the board had made appropria-
lions therefor This is haphazard and risky
way of running any business-and especially
business as large and important as the govern
ment of Arlington County


In brief, the auditors said, budget OPERA
tions have come to lag behind actual operations
Thus In practice, the cart has been put before
the horse and the budget has lost its value as
medium of financial and operating control
Various reasons were assigned for this situation.
including too centralized and overburdened &C
counting and Illustration and confusion" result
Ing from unclear responsibilities The necessity
Tor comprehensive overhaul and modernization
OF Arlington's bookkeeping and budgeting pro-
cedures is plainly indicated The post-election
board should give this reform priority over
routine problems.

ROME, Jan. 29.-Non- Com
munist newspapers today hailed
as signs of "Titoism" and a grave
crisis within the Italian Com
munist Party the resignation OF
two of its deputies. The Com
munist Party and it's newspapers
maintained a strict silence.


Neither L'Unita, official organ
of the Italian Communist Party
second largest in the world
nor "Avanti," organ of Commu-
notwithstanding Socialists, men
toned the designations.
Personal Motives Charged.
Rome's independent "Giornale
d'Italia" said the Red silence had
failed to minimize the episode,
which holds the center of polit-
ical comment and confirms re-
ports of grave internal crisis
in the Italian Communist Party"


The Communicating II Paese of
Rome said an official party an
nouncement is awaited. Mean
while, it charged the designations
stemmed from personal, not
political. motives.


The two deputies, Waldo Mag
mani, who was secretary of the
Communist Federation of Reggie
Emilia, and Aldo Cucchi of Be-
logna, said they left the party for
political reasons. Both come from
what has been considered Italy's
Communist stronghold.


Both Were Partisans.


Both were former partisan lead
erS during the war. Cucchi was
awarded the gold medal for brav-
cry - Italy's highest military
award.


The designations came while
party leader Palmiro Togliatti was
in Moscow. It has not been re-
vealed when or if he would return
to Italy. The annual Communist
Party national congress, originally
scheduled for this month, has been
postponed because of Togliatti's
brain operation two months ago.
There are now reports that it will
be postponed still further, pending
his possible return.

date.


Tabled as the No. 3 team in the

The Vols still play Tennessee

strong array. The Spartans face
Pitt, Notre Dame, Indiana and
Colorado in their final four games.


Actually. they're the only two

All the other preseason favorites

Alabama was rated high up in the

power of the West Coast outside
of California. and if the Golden
Bears stumbled just once. the
Huskies would grab the Pacific
Coast Conference title and a Rose
Bowl spot:


Where are they now? Kentucky
is hobbling along in eighth place
in the Southeastern loop, just
keeping its head above water,
while Alabama is last with three
league defeats and no triumphs.
1t has managed to win one game
outside conference competition.


Washington Stumbles.


California stumbled, all right.
but Washington wasn't there. 1t
was Southern California, which
could go right into the Rose Bowl.


Oklahoma. the national cham
pion last year, was pegged at No. 4
this time. but the Sooners have
played just 500 football with two
victories in four games. Colorado
is leading the Big Seven. a league
which doesn't have an undefeated
team.


Texas and Texas AIM also were
voted in the first 10 before the
season opened. They both have
been beaten once. and Texas is
No. 10 in this weeks AP poll. But
their one defeat each has been in
the Southwest Conference, which
means they'll have to go fast from
here in to overtake undefeated
Baylor.

country have been Georgia Tech.
Northwestern, Illinois and Prince

high in first place in the South

triumphs and no defeats. They've
also won one outside the league
and might give Tennesse fight
Tor the loop championship.


Princeton Still Winning.

gan leads the loop with two VIC

side play. Both the Illini and
Northwestern are undefeated in

And the situation will get pro-

This general review Of the sit
Iuation was confirmed today by
the State Highway Department.
The department put the blame
on two factors:


l. ALLEGATIONS made by the Fed
|eral Government for steel for new
road construction are too small.


Rubber Checks" Blamed.


2. The allocations, made quar-

For the third quarter Of this
year. the department reported, the

3,100 tons.

mills, the department revealed,

Of the Is persons still missing and

small patrol boats. State police
combed the shores on foot.


While this search went on. both
the Coast Guard and the Suffolk
County district attorney pushed
separate investigations into one of

The fishing boat, the Pelican,
keeled over in the stormy Atlantic

tip Of Long Island, 125 miles from
New York City. A boiling riptide
caught the 48-foot craft with one
of its tow engines dead.

q day of deep-sea fishing Satur-
day morning. using the Labor Day
week end for one last summer
outing.

ket shed were placed the 19 bodies
recovered from the sea and the
wrecked cabin of the Pelican.


The Coast Guard, which ex-
pressed doubt that any of the
missing were still alive, said many
of the bodies may never be found.
1t was believed the same rip tide
that hit the vessel had carried
the bodies out to sea.


The Pelican disaster brought a
debate among some survivors and
boat operators on whether the
small vessel was overloaded.


No Limit on Passengers.


The law does not limit the num-
Der of persons permitted to sail
on such craft, although regula-
tions specify there must be a life
preserver for each passenger. The
Pelican had Sc preservers.

Lindsay Henry said he did mot

mitted." However. he added that

jury"

urday. but the Coast Guard at
tributed the accident mainly to
the engine failure.

listed a total of 80 survivors and
one dead and five missing of the
SO crewmen.

sett radioed district headquarters
here that six men were found near
the scene of the disaster, some
300 miles off the Washington
coast, about 6 am, EST.
The rescue came after two
nights and one day of searching
A terse radio message said:


Missing lifeboat found with six
survivors. All are well and all
taken aboard"


One man was killed when the
grain-laden ship exploded and
caught fire late Tuesday. Five
others were lost during rescue
attempts by merchant vessels that
hurried to the scene.


The survivors, the Coast Guard
said, will be brought in as soon
as weather permits.


The Coast Guard cutter North
Wind was ordered to remain at
the scene and try to extinguish
the fire still burning on the Wal
ton and to tow her to port.

forces out of the Suez Canal zone.
Britain has served notice the
troops are staying.

clash to appear in Cairo news
papers said three British soldiers
and two Egyptian policemen were
killed. Later a British spokesman
said the three Egyptians were
killed but that there were no

Ell Din Pasha said one Briton had
been found dead, and a British
officer reported to the Suez gov
ernorate that two other British
soldiers had been killed. The
foreign minister said two Egyp-
tians were wounded.

SEOUL, Dec. l. delayed by
Censor)-The Korean government
today placed nearly one-third of
South Korea under martial law
and put two Of its top generals
in charge of a drive to wipe out
Red guerrillas.


The government entrusted the
drive to its best field commander.
Maj. Gen. PAX Sun Yup, who
developed the crack South Ko-
rean First division and now COM
mands the First Korean Corps.


1t. Gen. Lee Chong Chan, Ko-
rean Chief Of Staff, was placed in
overall direction.


The martial law decree en-
braces PuSan. southeast port city
and current South Korean capital.
Mysterious fires there within a
week have destroyed an arsenal
and the United States Embassy
building.


@@ oNSs SoAAP%ASAs


It will be the largest campaign
against guerrillas of the whole
war, although in the past United
States Marines have joined Ko-
rean police in operations against
the Red raiders.


The operation shaped up as a
major Korean government effort
to clean up the guerrillas once and
for all with overwhelming force.


The areas are we'll behind the
Allied lines. Included in the mar
tial law decree also is Taegu, AL
lied anchor in the old Pusan peri
meter early in the war.


Two veteran Korean divisions
were believed ready to go into
action. supported by the mobilized
national police and various re-
serve units.


Meanwhile Communist jets were
reported to have shot down four
Allied warplanes Saturday IN one
of the first Red victories Of the
Korean air war.


Fifth Air Force said the MIG
15s destroyed three Australian
Meteor jets and one American
F-80 Shooting Star. The Meteors
shot down two MICS and dam
aged three others.


The swirling air battle marked
the first time the Reds have shot
down as many as four Allied
planes in one day. The Allied loss
came just a day after the United
Nations greatest air victory Of
the war: II Red planes shot down,
one probably destroyed and three |
damaged.


Ground Action Quiet.
The Australian planes - twin |
jet Gloster Meteors from Great
Rpitain-are early model jets. |
roughly comparable to the Ameri-
can Shooting Star. Both are
slower than the MICS.


In addition, the 5th Air Force
said q Marine fighter was shot
down by Red ground fire.


The ground war remained quiet.


Allied casualties were extremely
light. The exact figure was with
held, but across the entire las
mile front the manpower loss was
much less than one battalion
might lose in a single hill attack.

way up.

explained. smoke does not expand

immigration officials have said

Suddenly, great, bull-should-

Zucchini, that Italian darling
of the squash family, becomes
decorative as well as delectable
when prepared in fan-fashion.


Buy one young zucchini for
each person. Peel them as you
would cucumbers. then parboll
them in sailed water to which a
little lemon juice has been added.
Drain them and dry them care
fully with cloth. When they
are cold slice them lengthwise to
within an inch of the end, press

out fanwise. Sprinkle them with
flour, salt and pepper, and fry to
a delicate brown, turning carefully
to brown both sides. Pour over
them, after putting them on a
dish, the melted butter from the
pan, with more lemon juice and
some chopped parsley. Serve

PHILADELPHIA, Jan. 1.-The

and danced today as millions
watched Philadelphia's tradition

New Year.


Reinforced by more than a
million spectators in holiday

heart of the city for the day.
Two television stations gave hun
dreds of thousands of watchers
a freside view Of the annual show.


Crystal clear weather and a
bright sun brought out all the
colors and spangles of costumes
splendid In their feathers and
fancy work. Block-long capes Of
the fancy clubs rippled in the
breeze and lifting tunes echoed
through skyscraper canyons as the
string bands marched and counter
marched through their carefully
planned maneuvers.


All along the 10-miIe parade
route up Broad street, around
city hall and then east toward
the river, grown-upS and kids
lined 3 to 10 deep along the curbs.


Regular traffic was shooed
around the parade route by aug
mented police traffic details, or
stood blocked at crossings. AS the
first units strobe past the judges
stand others still were waiting TO
fall in line at the starting point
and the parade seemed certain to
carry far into the afternoon.


Mr.. and Mrs. Philadelphia and
their children and guests had to
bundle warmly for protection
against near-freezing tempera-
lures, but nobody seemed to mind,
least of all the mummers.


Some of the paraders were
warmed by their efforts to man
age bulky fancy costumes. but
others wore very little indeed and
seemed not to mind the cold at
all.

the control room. He shouted to

son, under life sentence for the
shooting of a State policeman. The
convicts carried a wooden gun
screw drivers, ice picks and similar

17-14) and in 1949 against North

BELGRADE, Yugoslavia, Sept.
13.-Premier- Marshal Tito is har-
vesting new crop Of worries
this fall in the form of sharply
increased border hostility, frontier
shootings and spy activities by his
prof. Russian neighbors.


In the past seven months there
have been 837 border incidents
along Yugoslavia's frontier with
Albania. Bulgaria, Romania and
Hungary. This is nearly one-third
of the total for the entire period
since Tito's break with the Comm
form in June, 1948.


The increased tempo of the
Cominform's border pressure -
particularly in the last 10 days.
has raised the question: Do Russia
and her puppet states mean busi-
ness this time? Are the new in
cidents a prelude to invasion?


No one knows the answer for
certain except the Kremlin, and
it isn't talking.


Short Step From War.


Yugoslavia and the Cominform
countries appeared only a short
step from actual war as they gath
cred in late fall crops-bringing
to mind the old Balkan adage
that wars begin when crops are
in"


Trade between Yugoslavia and
her Eastern neighbors ended
completely more than a year and
a half ago.


Diplomatic relations have been
reduced to exchanges of insults,
accusations and formal notes
protesting various incidents
These notes usually are rejected.
denied or calmly ignored.


Diplomatic staffs-both those
maintained by the Cominform
countries here and those repre-
senting YugoSlavia in the Com
inform capitals-have been re-
duced to skeleton size. They are
under constant surveillance by the
security police in each country.
Their chief function now is to
gather what information they
can about the political, economic
and military affairs in the coun-
try Their source of information
lis limited largely to what they
can read in newspapers.


All along Yugoslavia'S twisting
eastern and southern frontiers,
both sides have posted countless
Thousands of border guards.


In the danger spots, such as the
major travel routes across the
frontiers. barbed wire entangle-
ments, pillboxes, recently dug
trenches and outlook towers en-
phasize the border tension.


Behind border outposts are
concentrated heavy units Of sea-
soned troops. On the Yugoslav
side they probably are most num-
erous on the Bulgarian border.
since military men long have re-
garded that as the chief danger
spot


Refugees from iron curtain
countries tell of widespread prep
arations which have the earmarkS
of preparations for attack-or at
least of measures to furnish that
impression.


CiviIianS Evacuated


These reports range from the
wholesale evacuation of civilians
from an area 20 miles deep in
Bulgaria and Romania to wide
spread activity by Russians direct.
ing military training and the con-
Istruction of military establish
Iments, such as a new air base near
Sofia.


Despite controls, a two-way
traffic of refugees and spies flows
across the border. Yugoslavia
naturally asserts a top-heavy per-
Icentage of that traffic has been
coming in her direction. COMM
form propaganda says just the
contrary.


The outcome may well depend
on these three factors:


/. The Kremlin's decision on
whether an invasion of Yugoslavia
would touch off World War III.


2. How soon and how much
military aid Yugoslavia can get
from the West,

decided to put the seven league
members on record as opposing
Communism and backing the
same principles as the Western
democracies.

economic aid.

the league council when the
council convenes Monday.

league security pact built around

Five-year-old Sheila Ann Foley
died today in Arlington Hospital
of burns received May 2 while
playing with matches.


Sheila Ann, daughter of Mr.. and
Mrs. James B. Foley of 4311 South
Twelfth road, Arlington, was try
ing to light candles that had been
bought in preparation for her
sixth birthday next week. The
matches ignited her clothing.


Neighbors wrapped blanket
about her after she ran screaming
from her apartment residence.


Mrs. Foley said her daughter
apparently had taken the matches
and candles from the kitchen, un-
known to any one else. Sheila
apparently got the idea from a
birthday party she had attended
"a few days earlier at a palymate's
home, her mother said.

TUSCALOOSA, Ala, Aug. 16.-
The desperate crime-laden flight
of. three young Alabama convicts
has brought a death sentence to
one and life imprisonment to the
others.


A Tuscaloosa Circuit Court jury
last night convicted 16-year-old
Fred Noe, the youngest, of raping
a 40-year-old Tuscaloosa house
wife. The jury fixed his sentence
at life.


Several hours earlier Johnny
Mack Rogers, II, had pleaded
guilty to robbery and also been
given life.


Charles Campbell, %, was sem
fenced to death Monday.


Noe and Campbell were accused
of raping Mrs. Ernest w. Garner
after bursting into her home while
she was bathing.


The three were captured in
Delhi, La, after a three-day
flight.


Noe was serving three years and
three days for burglary and grand
larceny when he and the others
escaped June 13. Rogers was
under sentence of eight years and
one day for burglary, and Camp
bell two years for grand larceny.

visit in Norway.

tiations broke down early last
year. the ration of meat to Brit
iSh homes was cut to the lowest
| in history.

ments to Britain will be frozen
beef. About 10000 tons are ready

ports Immediately. Argentina

ments could start today.

tionally gets the same price as

gotiations which started sever

slugger with his roundhouse
swings during the latter stages as
Williams seemed to tire.

METZ, France, Aug. 24.-The
Basel Calais Express rammed into
the rear of a Frankfurt-Pari
train near here today. Ten per-
sons, including two Americans,
were killed, and possibly 40 others,
about half Of them United States
soldiers, were injured.


The two soldiers killed were
Identified as Alphonse MacLaugh-
lin of Durham. N. c., and Everett
~ Whalon of Norwich, Conn.
United States Army headquarters
said the injured Americans were
sent to the 98th General Hospital
at Munich. Germany.


Seventeen French soldiers were
among the injured.


The express from Frankfurt,
Germany, had just passed the
Sanry-sur-Nied station, 10 miles
from Metz. The engineer halted
the train on safety signal. The
Paris-bound train was 80 minutes
late.


The train from Basel, Switzer-
land, proceeding at about so miles
an hour, rammed into the wooden
car at the end of the Frankfurt
train, smashing the car to bits
and pushing the next one, a Sec
ond-class carriage, on to the roof
of the car ahead.


United States military police
from Metz were rushed to the
scene. American headquarters at
Orleans, France. said officers were
investigating reports that the bag
gage and mail cars of the trains
had been pillaged, but other Unit
ed States Army officials nearer the
scene said they had no informa-
ton on this, and French police
denied the report.

These are vacation days and perhaps
one might lawfully digress from the
heavier news. Anyhow. the ancient as
tronomers really gave this sultry sum-
mer period its name, dies caniculares,"
which means dog days all right but the
Latin sounds a lot more elegant than our
English sounds But the term, in any
language is unfair. Sirius, the big Dog
Star, rose along with Orion, the far
famed hunter with his three-star buckle,
about evening in July for the Romans,
with Procyon, the little Dog Star, coming
up on the right, and they all travel up
from the east together.


Just because the weather happened to
be hot and humid about then, the
ancients blamed it on the dogs-a period
from 20 days before to 20 days after
the rising of the big Dog Star, Sirius, at
present reckoned from July 3 to Au-
gust II.


We might, as gentle and impeccable
Americans, make fair concession and
call these days not the less elegant
name, "dog days." but the more elegant
dies caniculares."

Mrs. Jessie Moon Hoton, who died on
Wednesday at IS, was school teacher in the
great tradition. She started classes in her own
home here more than half century ago. Hen
main capital was the force of her own person.
atty. She respected intellectual achievement
and she based her school on the idea that young
women could learn anything that young men
could learn. She respected their personalities
as individuals, but she had a larger ideal: She
felt that there was no substitute for personal
quality In an individual. She taught high
standards of honor and integrity and public
responsibility.


Generations of girls went to her school, came
away and found they had been touched by more
than the merely academic. They sent their
daughters and their granddaughters, and Mrs.
Holton's classes for young ladies became the
present-day Holton-Arms School and Junior
College.


Always an idealist Mrs. Holton also could
be intensely practical It was a mission Of her
later years that she should leave her school
(Which has been for years a non-proft organi-
zation) so that 1t would continue without inter-
ruption after her death. She slipped quietly
away from its active operation some time ago,
but she had left her stamp upon it and upon
the thousands of useful public spirited Washing
ton women who were her pupils

Salaries of baseball players are
included in the wage freeze, law
yers for the Wage Sterilization
Board said yesterday.


They hastily pointed out, how
ever, that this doesn't mean that
every baseball player necessarily
will perform this summer for the
same pay that he got last year.


But they said that as the situa-
ton stands right now, players
salaries are frozen.


One of the boards lawyers
M. L. Mike" Ryder-said the
baseball players case can best be
illustrated by an example. Ryder
told a reporter:


Suppose a doctor or a dentist
is working for himself, charging
fees for his work. He's exempt.


But suppose he's working for
a company, on a yearly basis. He's
covered in the wage freeze along
with other wage earners.'


Baseball players have one break
Although they are signing con-
tracts now, their pay doesn't start
until the season begins.


The wage board lawyers said
that undoubtedly by that time
many exceptions to the wage
freeze will have been made.

UNITED STATES 9th ARMY
HEADQUARTERS, Korea. Aug. 16.
South Korea's expanding army
next week will begin intensive re-
training under American officers
in one of the most unusual pro-
grams ever attempted during a
war.


They will be brought a few
miles out of the front lines for
about eight weeks of basic train
ing in military tactics.


One division will be pulled out
at time, and none will leave its
general battle sector.


If the Kaesong ceaSe-f1re talks
should collapse and the Com
munists hurl another offensive at
the United Nations, the Republic
of Korea Division could be moved
right back into the line.


The American Korean Military
Advisory Group has been reor-
ganized and expanded during the
past few months to handle the
program. Most of the instructors
have been serving with ROW di-
visions since the war began.


Some have moved into the
training area.


Caught by Surprise.


The South Korean forces
numbered about 10000 electives
when the war began June 25, 1850.
They were lightly equipped, poorly
trained and caught completely by
surprise when the North Koreans
hurled their Russian trained
troops across the 38th Parallel.
Within one week the broken ROK
units were in retreat southwark.
Some fought valiantly against
overwhelming odds to stem the
Communists until American help
arrived.


Remnants of this disorganized.
force struggled into the Pusian
perimeter. Their equipment was
gone. Many of its best officers were
dead. Shortages of weapons made
the task of re-equipping troops
slow and tedious.


In the language of the soldier,
there was a constant demand for
bodies" to replace the casualties.
Some Koreans became soldiers"
by firing carbine once. They were
thrust into the line with less than
week of training. ROK divisions
collapsed several times at critical
periods in the war. But they held
most OF the northern line of the
perimeter during those grim days.


The 9th Army tried to integrate
South Korean soldiers into United
Nations units. The plan was
never wholly successful. Ian
guage was the main difficulty.


9Th Division Broke.


During the months of smashing
Allied victories in the dash toward
the Yalu River, there was neither
time nor inclination to properly
train the South Koreans. They
were given gun, put into a di-
vision and told to head north.


Need for strengthening the
ROK divisions was brought home
forcefully last April. The Chinese
and North Koreans started their
first spring offensive against AL
lied positions. The ROK 9th di- |
vision broke and ran. leaving
dangerous hole that American
forces finally plugged in bitter |.
hand d-to-hand fighting.


The 9Th Army under Gen. James
A. Van Fleet began studies for
retraining and reorganizing the
South Korean divisions. KMAG
was rapidly expanded to handle
the job.


Brig. Gen. C. E. Ryan, COM
manding officer of KMAG, went
to the United States for special
training before taking over his
new assignment. A replacement
training school center for the
South Korean army was started.


Brig. Gen. S. Champeny is COM
manding officer of the replace
ment training and school center.


The field training phase of the
new program will be headed by
Brig. Gen. Thomas Cross.


The instruction will be strenu-
Gus. 1t will be patterned after
the basic training given American
soldiers back home.

Something should be done promptly to cor
rect gross injustice affecting new employees Of
the Post Office Department. These employees are
being unfairly deprived of all annual and sick
leave benefits and pension privileges. They are
the only group of employees in the Government
suffering such discrimination


The situation results from combination Of
laws and administrative orders. The leave act,
passed long before the present emergency, spe-
cifcally excludes temporary postal employees
from taking annual or sick leave. At that time
Temporary workers meant those hired during
the Christmas rush period. Now, however, under
the Whitten amendment and under subsequent
presidential order, all newly hired employees are
classified as "temporary'-even though their en-
ployment in the end may prove to be quite per-
manent. Most temporary" employees are en-
titled to leave just as regular civil service per-
sonnel are But the new employees of the Post
Office Department. however permanent their
Jobs may turn out to be- are excluded by reason
of legislation that obviously was not intended to
apply in the present emergency.


The pension inequity comes about through
social security law amendment giving pension
rights to all temporary employees hired during
the emergency excepting non-classif1ed postal
workers. Why these postal employees were ruled
out of the amendments provisions has never been
explained. No good reason is apparent for this
discriminatory policy, nor for depriving new
postal personnel of vacations and sick leave.
Congress and the Civil Service Commission ought
to give this problem early attention.

have not taken up other matters.


Among problems scheduled to
be presented today are municipa,
revenue raising schemes and
proposals from the county Civic
Federation's Legislative Commit

Mayors Of seven incorporated
towns are to ask that the county
return part of its real estate tax
income derived from municipal
residents for police protection.


They also will ask for a special
fire tax on unincorporated areas
served by the towns fire depart

TAIPEH. Formosa. Dec. 10
Two years ago today Generals
simo Chang Kai-shek and his
Nationalist government fed main
land China for Formosa, one
jump ahead of advancing Chinese
Communist armies.


Nearly every one here thought
then that the Reds would capture
Formosa within few months and
that Chang and the Nationalists
would be finished.


Any one predicting that Chang
would still be holding this island
of the southeast coast Of China
two years later would have been
considered an idle dreamer.


But today Chang still holds
Formosa and talks of returning to
the mainland.


The turning point in Chiang's
fortunes came June 27, 1866
two days after the outbreak of the
Korean war. when President Tru-
man assigned the United States
7th Fleet to safeguard Formosa
from Communist invasion.


Another important event was
the creation last summer of a
United States military assistance
advisory group to build up a
Nationalist combat force.

BERLIN, Aug. 13. - German
Communist youth bosses publicly
hailed Prime Minister Stain to-
day as their "Fuehrer." They did
this in a message to the Soviet
leader following up yesterdays
screaming parade of Communist
youth, demonstration which far
outdid anything the Nazis ever
whipped up for Hitler.


But the West used the Commu-
mist world youth festival to get
in some propaganda blows of it's
own. Hundreds of thousands of
youngsters who slipped by the Red
guards on the sector border saw
things in "imperialist" West Ber-
lin they never dreamed existed
there.


The leaders of the Communist
Free German Youth Movement
(FDJ used the word "Fuehrer
Qeader) r)-once applied exclusively
to Hitler-when they sent the So
Wet Prime Minister a pledge
promising undying loyalty to him
and unfailing opposition to
western imperialists.' Time
after time the message. purport-
edly signed by 4,145,839 young
Germans, addressed the Soviet
leader as Dear Joseph Stain. -
1t concluded with the words:
Long live our wise teacher and
Fuehrer, our best friend, the great
Stain"


Million Sent Home.


More than a million hoarse
and footsore Communist youths
were sent home today after they
screamed praise of Stain for
hours in yesterdays parade, the
climaxing event of the youth
festival.


At once youngsters resumed
their secret invasion of West Ber-
lin, with it's capitalistic lures. One
special attraction was the open
ing today of an American tele-
vision exhibit. Something new
even for West Berliners, the tele-
vision shows in color and in black
and white obviously amazed the
Iron Curtain youngsters.


Against such competition the
Communist World Youth Festival,
continuing for another week in
East Berlin, looked even drabber.

"A missing 21-year-old nurse
with an interest in fasting, walked
out of mountain wilderness in
apparent good condition last night

two weeks wandering without food
or protection.


The nurse, Evangeline Lorimer
was taken to a hospital at nearby
ISevieryille for observation but
rangers said she was suffering
mainly from puffed feet and insect
bites. They said she showed nc
signs of malnutrition.


Robert White, acting superin-
itendent of the Smoky Mountains
National Park, said she apparently
was only half lost during the per-
iod when search parties were plod-
ding over the rugged terrain. He
quoted her as saying she had
heard them but didn't have the
energy to respond.


She was located on little trail

in the general area where she dis
appeared June 8. She told Rangers
| she had decided it was time to
come out"


On the basis of her story to
Rangers. the intensely religious
nurse ate no food during the two
weeks. Mr.. White said he had
learned she had experimental
with fasting at nursing school and
had shown unusual interest in
Ivitamins and concentrated foods.
Her father, w. H. Lorimer, an
evangelist. insisted she carried no
food away from camp.


The Ranger said her story was
confused, but he delayed pressing
questions upon her until after doc
tors give approval. Her account
was that she saw no human being
during her walk. She brayed the
fastness in a tee shirt, jeans and
low white shoes. She had no coat
nor blankets to protect her from
the torrential rains that fell dur
ing the period or the cool mountain
nights.


She drank from the numerous
swift streams in the area.
She was an experienced hiker
At the time she wandered into
the parks bear-infested thickets
lalong the Tennessee-N North Caro-
lima border, she was on a camp
ing trip with her father in the
Cades Cove area.


An unidentified mountain boy
spotted her on Hannah Mountain
last night and escorted her to q
warden station. She was about

good account of the days and indi-

lin one of the canyons. She kept

A few days ago took a drive in the
country and I thought perhaps some of
your city-bound readers might like to
share the beauty saw. chose hilly
road and on the crests could see the
slate-blue highway stretching away in
the distance like a long ribbon with a
green satin stripe through the middle
and in the little valleys it was shady and
damp and cool. The deep blue Of the
sky was decorated with great masses of
powder-puf clouds and some Of the
clusters looked like sprays of white roses
tied together with lacy streamers. A re.
cent rain had washed the air crystal
clear. fresh and sweet.


Green loveliness of many hues spread
out as far as the eye could see over
woodland and field. In soft breeze the
trees stretched their limbs against each
other and rustled their leaves, and
seemed to whisper secrets not meant for
man to hear.


The locusts. and their graceful SOUTH
ern cousins, the mimosas, Swayed and
ratified their seed pods nervously as
though they could hardly wait for sharp
winds to snap loose the heavy beans and
scatter them on the ground. Silver ma
Piles turned up their leaves, to flaunt
their shining color and brag about their
silver wealth to less glamorous neigh
bors. Sycamores, with patches Of white
bark cleaning through their yellowish
green foliage, stood stiff and straight
and hardly bowed at all in the wind,
and here and there the weeping willows
dragged their lovely tresses on the
ground. wondered what primeval sor-
row could have lain in the heart of a
tree so lovely that it should deserve so
sad name.


Great patches of cone and heart
shaped cedars came into view, and now
and then pine tree matched its per-
manent. dark green beauty against the
taller oaks and NAPLES, hickories and
elms. There were many kinds Of trees
and shrubs whose names did not know,
but they gave loveliness to the land
scape, and, I am sure, usefulness to the
soil.


In the shady stretches, rows of the
tall Joe-Pye weed, with beautiful clusters
Of deep magenta blooms, lined both sides
OF the road and bowed gracefully In the
breeze, disturbing the yellow butterflies
that hovered over the sweet blossoms

BASTAD, Sweden, July %
Sweden won the European Zone
Davis Cup tennis title today, but
not before it encountered stiff
opposition and engaged in a
comic-opera routine of tempera-
ment with its German rivals.


The Swedes, Lennart Bergelin
and Sven Davidson, took the
doubles today. 81, 81, 80,
60, after having swept yester-
days two singles matches. The
three triumphs make tomorrow's
two concluding singles matches
exhibitions.


After today's first three rugged
sets the Swedes walked off the
court for the usual intermission.
This apparently caught Baron
Gottfried Won Cramm and part
ner Roelf Goepfert by surprise.
They demanded that the match
be forfeited to them. The referee
disagreed.


But when the SwedeS returned
to the court, the Germans walked
away. Then it was the Swedes'
turn to claim forfeit. Again
the referee disagreed.


Finally the harassed official got
both teams back on the court at
the same time and play was re-
sumed. Sweden quickly romped to
an easy victory in contrast to the
previous three rugged sets.


BY its victory. Sweden gained
the right to meet the North Amer
ican Zone winner, probably the
United States, for the right to
challenge Australia for the inter-
national trophy. The Australians
won the cup year ago.


Date and site of the interzone
have not been set. Aus
tralia hopes they will be played
there early in December. The
challenge round is set for Mel
bourne December 1928.

For the first time Wet Mimi
forces took to the field during
daylight to hold back the relief
columns. the report said.


French bomber and fighter
planes flew 80 sorties today in
support of ground troops.

Chamber of Commerce.

retary of state, led the parade.

band, a calliope and four school
and Scout bands.


Torchlights carried by more
than 100 school children lighted

Chase Rescue Squad and the
Bethesda and Chevy Chase fire
departments also participated.
Dozens Of. floats depcited Christ
mas scene, a unit of 20 antique
automobiles and submarine float
sponsored by the Montgomery
County organized Naval Reserve
also were in the line of march.


Bringing up the rear was
Bethesda Chevy Chase High
Schools 70-member band, which
advertised itself as "the best band
out of uniform" Members wore
a motley assortment of apparel.
including barrels. bird cages and
paper uniforms. The band is
seeking funds for uniforms.

| BONN. Germany, Dec. 3.-Some
Allied occupation authorities are
thinking about resurrecting the
German arms industry to help
equip Atlantic defense forces.


With American arms output
tagging, some influential occupa-
ton officials are suggesting that
the West must tap the rich indus
trial Ruhr for armaments along
with German manpower to tip the
military balance against Russia.
A responsible source said today
one Allied leader in Germany
already has proposed to his gov
ernment that the West should per-
NIT full-scale German arms pro-
duction again. He declined to
identify the official or his govern
ment.


This source said the arguments
of officials. who favor hitching the
Ruhr to the Vests arms drive,
run like this:


Mass production of tanks,
artillery and other equipment by
the Ruhr would speed up the
equipping of IL German divisions
planned for the European army.


The Germans could also help
equip the armies of Italy, Belgium
and The Netherlands, which are
receiving weapons from Canada
and the United States:


This would insure Britain and
France priority on American arms
shipments.


The source emphasized that the
question of tapping the Ruhr for
armament production had not
progressed beyond the talking
stage. 1t is certain to encounter
stiff opposition from many quar-
terS.


Must Start From Scratch.


The informant said some high
ranking officials here fear the cost
of arming German contingents
for European army may be pro-
hibitive, unless the Germans are
allowed to produce their own
equipment.


The Germans must start from
scratch. They lack barracks,
training grounds and even uni
forms. Under present plans, the
western poWers-principally the
United StateS-muSt supply all
equipment and part of the cost of
recruiting and training German
divisions under these conditions.


German leaders estimate the
first years cost of creating II di-
visions at Sc billion. But some
Allied sources put the figure at
$l4 billion.


So. suggestions are being made
in Allied circles that it would be
to the interest of the western pow
ers if the Germans produced their
own arms instead of having other
nations supplying them.

PUSAN, Korea, Nov. 30.-The
Korean government arsenal here
blew up today in a series of awe
some blasts that spread damage
across an area 4 miles wide.


American soldiers housed in the
general area escaped injury. but
United States Army authorities
said six Koreans were killed and
at least so were injured.


Korean authorities said 48
homes were destroyed, 100 others
were badly damaged and 400 more
were damaged in some degree.
They estimated total damage at
$40 million.


Civilian and army rescue work.
ers dug in the ruins searching for
possibly more victims.


Col. Lee Hong Chong. chief of
the arsenal, said it was not known
whether sabotage or accident
touched off the blasts that rocked
this southeast port city and sent
civilians racing from their homes
in panic.


Embassy Destroyed Monday.


1t was recalled, however, that
a mysterious fire destroyed the
United States Embassy building
in Pusan Monday. The North
Korean Reds long have boaSted
they have agents in Pusan.


Col. Lee said the arsenal, on
Pusan's northern outskirts, was
closed for the night and only
guards were on duty.


The first explosion came at 4
am. Ammunition was blown high
in the air and exploded in a tre-
mendous fireworks display. Then
came a second blast and a series
OF smaller ones. Giant flames
licked the sky.


Debris WhiStled through the air
and. with the tremendous blast.
leveled dwellings clustered around
the arsenal.


Defense Minister Lee Kee Poong
appealed for United Nations civil
assistance relief for the homeless,
many of them war refugees.


The Hiahleah housing center for
the United States Army was in
the blast area. Some windows
there were blown out, but author
1tles said there were no casualties.

latter application of the Cape

vided in the Capehart amendment,

WEST CENTRAL FRONT,
Korea. April 26 Delayed Three
American battalions fought their
way out of encirclement yester-
day with almost incredible feats
of valor.


There was the captain who was
wounded nine times and still
wouldn't quit fighting. And the
two soldiers who had never fired
an artillery piece before. But
they blazed away at point-blank
range with 105-mm. howitzer.


The two infantry battalions and
one artillery battalion. normally
2,700 men, were covering the
withdrawal of an Allied column
down a narrow, dusty Korean
road.


Then came ambush.


Two Tanks Knocked Out.


Without warning Communist
soldier stepped onto the road firing
a machinegun. He riddled the
lead truck, blocking the road.


A relief column of tanks was
blasted. Two were knocked out.
The encirclement was completed.
The relief force was stopped.


The Chinese on the ridges of
the ravineS Swarmed down. Ma
chineguns, small arms and NOR
tarS opened up on the Ameri-
cans. But there was no panic.


Corpl. Bernard Combs and Pfc.
Nicola D. Ferrina had never fired
an artillery piece.


They manned los and fired it'll
point blank at the charging Chi
nese. They fired more than Isl
rounds in Is minutes. When their
company pulled out under a hail
of fire they spiked the howitzer
with a grenade.


Ferrina would not even talk
about it. Combs just said, "It
was the only thing to do"


Captain Wounded Nine Times.


An infantry captain, wounded
twice earlier in the ambush, kept
fighting and directing his men.
A Communist stepped into the
open with burp gun and hit the
captain seven more times.
The captain remained on his
feet leading his men until blood
covered his uniform.


Capt. Haywood Thomas and
Corpl. Joseph Frazier forced the
wounded captain down and put
him aboard the tanks.


Pvt. Norman Duty killed the
Communist burp gunner with a.
hand grenade. a


An infantry lieutenant jumped
on tank to man its exposed So
caliber machinegun. Two Chi
nese bullets hit him and knocked
him from the guns. Despite his
wounds he, stayed on his feet and
helped other wounded. He was
at the wheel of a truck when the
column took to a side road and
fought its way back to United
States lines.

Four military prisoners who

rarily housed in a stockade while
the guardhouse is being reno

heaviest earthquake ever recorded
on the volcano island of Hawaii

Ipf its treasured water stores

DrieSt Part of Islands.

water to the ocean floor.

impending eruption by Mauna Loa

VOLCANOES. It spilled molten lava

year ago.

at kailua, on the Kona coast, SAID
fire department and Hawaii Coun-
Ity trucks from 'Hilo. across the

tinue daily. The Kona coast nor
mally receives no rain until well
into October.

been little rain through July and
August. The hauled water must
be boiled for drinking purposes.

injured.

General Counsel Bott of the National Labor

Hartley Act. The provision is that which pre-
scribes the conditions for a union shop, and
which protects an employe from being dismissed
from his union and thereafter fired for any
reason except non-payment OF initiation fees
and dues.

from the union and the union members said they

was fired

In the ancient and glittering

ist class accommodations sold

UNITED STATES 9th ARMY
HEADQUARTERS, Korea, Nov. Z.
Allied troops attacking through
the mud today recaptured one of
three hills lost to Chinese assaults
since Sunday.


The Reds did not put up much
Of a fight to keep the peak north
west of Yonchon. Two battalions
Of Chinese had overrun it Tues
day.


The Reds drove United Nations
infantrymen out of advanced posi-
tions northwest of Korangpo, near
the 38th Parallel on the western
front. The Allies promptly coun-
terattacked and ran the Reds back
to their own lines.


Rain Impedes Fighting.


Elsewhere along the western
sector rain dampened the savage
infantry fighting of the past three
days. Artillery duels thundered
along the sector as the U. N. tried
to soften up Chinese still holding
two peaks they seized Sunday.


Red gunners knocked out five
Allied tanks on the east-central
front.


Storms deprived attacking Allied
troops in the west of all-out air
support Tuesday. A dispatch from
the front said improved weather
might signal another all-out drive
to push the Reds off the hills.


U. N. Command artillery has
been pounding Communist posi-
tions continuously. Communist
guns have been almost as active.
An 9th Army spokesman said
S.263 mortar and artillery shells
landed in Allied positions Tues
day.


Americans Regain Hills.


After the first Communist as
sault in the Yonchon area Sunday.
the fighting spread along a 20
mile front to a point a few miles
west of Chorwon, key Allied
strongpoint betwene the western
and west-central fronts. Ameri-
can troops were showed off two hill
positions in this sector early
Tuesday, but later reoccupied both
points against only light enemy
resistance.


The weather kept most Allied
warplanes on the ground Tuesday.
Far East Air Force headquar-
ters said only 230 sorties were
flown.


The battleship New Jersey, the
heavy cruiser Toledo and other
Allied warships poured shells onto
Communist supply lines along the
east coast.


Fliers from the Australian car
rier Sydney and British and
Canadian warships hammered
Communist gun positions on the
west coast.

Charts and statistical tables in the latest

Metropolitan Area show the urgent need for

Federal Bureau of Roads, leaves no doubt as to
such a shortage The report reveals that the
Anacostia River bridges carry considerably less
traffic than the Potomac bridges, yet the Ana
costa has more crossing facilities than the river
of which it is branch.


The survey analyzed in the report was made
In 1948 Since then the amount of traffic over
both rivers has increased substantially. The
increase over the Potomac has been particularly
noteworthy because of the large residential de-
velopments in nearby Virginia since 1948. AND
the problem will become even more acute Win
the construction of new national airport at,
Burke Most of the airport traffic will be fun
neled into Shirley Highway and thence onto the
Fourteenth street bridge.


There are now only four bridges connecting
Washington with the Virginia suburbs They are
the new Fourteenth street bridge, with its prede-
cessor the old Highway bridge Eventually to be
replaced by twin of the new bridge), the Me-
mortal Bridge linking the Lincoln Memorial with
Arlington National Cemetery, the Key Bridge



Bridge. which carries Canal road traffic to the
Virginia shore near the Arlington-Fairfax line.
The AnacoStia. on the other hand is spanned
by bridges at South Capitol street, Eleventh
street Southeast, Pennsylvania avenue South
east and Benning road Northeast. Construction
of new bridge at East Capitol street has been
begun, and another bridge across the stream
is planned as part of the Washington-Balti-
more Parkway project.


comparison of traffic loads crossing the two
rivers supports the contention that the Ana
costa has received favored treatment, despite
less traffic. Traffic across the Potomac River
rose from a little over 100000 vehicles in "a
hours during 1910 to more than 10000 vehicles
In 1949. The increase for the Anacostia bridges
was from more than 10000 a day in 1910 to
slightly less than 100000 in 1949. The rush-hour
traffic count two years ago was $4,000 cars an
hour for the Potomac and $4,000 an hour for
the Anacostia.


These figures justify the emphasis which

Capital Park and Planning Commission and
other agencies have begun to place on the need

tualy will be necessity, too. Until the Potomac
bridge shortage is relieved, the bottleneck condi

existing crossings will continue to be the despair
of motorists and traffic authorities.
