Not content with monopolizing the main
event, New York has opened World Series
sideshow that rivals the big show itself as an
end-of-the season baseball attraction. The
play-of for the National League pennant be-
tween the Brooklyn Dodgers and the New York
Giants may have an anticlimactic effect on the
final showdown for baseballs championship.


Certainly baseball, being crowded from the
sports scene by collegiate and professional foot
ball, has determined to bow out in blaze Of
excitement Interest of the fans outside of New
York would have Jagged if each league had pro-
duced an easy winner, each from the big city.
But the Yankees were forced to fight until the
last stages of the American League campaign
and the National League battle turned into one
of the most breath taking in baseball history
Only last August the Dodgers seemed to be
safely out in front of all contenders in the older
circuit, with lead of 1871 games. Then things
began to happen. The Giants began to win
games with amazing regularity and the margin
separating them from the Buns dwinded.


Yesterday came the crucial test for both
contenders. Each needed win to remain in
the race. If both won, tie would result The
Giants took close one from the Boston Braves
and Brooklyn fought 1t out with the Phillies
for IA nerve-racking innings before home run
by Jackie Robinson gave the Dodgers the deci-
sion, 9-6. For many sports lovers the struggles
of the New York teams overshadowed the tele-
vised football game of the Redskins, who lost a
lively contest to the Detroit Lions, and the final
games of the luckless Mats, who divided a
double header at Griffith Stadium The play-off
in New York will be -out-of-three affair.
Chances are the little series will draw crowds
as large as the inter-league playoff, which
begins next Thursday. Any way one looks at it,
the Yankees are sitting pretty. Already favored
for the championship, they can rest while their
prospective opponents use up their energy in
trying to beat each other.

With the approach of cold
weather. farmers should give spe-
cial attention to winterizing en-
gines on their farms.


According to Guy w. Gienger.
associate extension agricultural
engineer of the University Of
Maryland. this means changing
oil more frequently, keeping the
battery fully charged and using
approved type anti-freeze.


However. Mr.. Gienger states.
greater attention should be given
to winterizing small engines that
are not normally used during the
cold season. Such engines are
found on combines. balers, spray
rigs. garden tractors and even
lawn mowers. An engine that
runs well today. he warns. may
not be in operating condition next
spring unless it is properly pre-
pared for winter.


To winterize an engine: Drain
the oil and replace with new oil,
clean the air cleaner and fill with
clean oil. check the spacing. on
spark plugs and breaker points,
pour about two ounces of light
oil in each spark plug hole, drain
the gas tank. carburetor, radiator
and engine block. turn over the
engine few times. with the igni-
ton off, to distribute the light oil
around the valves and piston
rings.

BALTIMORE, Dec. 25.-Highly
paid Don Barksdale, the ALL
America player from UCLA, who
has been something of pro dis
appointment. is under indefinite
suspension by the Baltimore Bull
lets basketball team.


Neither the club nor Barksdale
would give a reason for the sus-
pension, which came yesterday.


The first announcement was
that the 6-foot-6 Negro from Oak
land was on the inactive list, and
later the suspension was an
nounced. Jim Owens was recalled
from the Washington Caps to re-
place him.


Barksdale's salary with the Bull
lets never has been announced,
but the club says it is the highest
ever paid an athlete in Baltimore.
Figures between $4,000 and $20,-
900 have been reported. He was
twice All-America at UCLA,
played on the United States
Olympic team in 1948 and the
an-American team last year. He
also was with the Oakland Bitt-
ners and the Blue and Gold AAU
championship team before the
Bullets induced him to turn pro.


Early in the season Barksdale
complained of foot soreness, and
has played very little, while aver
aging 10 points a game.

customary morning devotionS.


The Puritans were stern folk who left
little leeway for recreation and who had

traditions of England. But William

STUTTGART. Germany, Dec
8. - Three Southwest German
states vote tomorrow on this issue


Should they unite into, one big
state? Or should they go back
to their prewar division into two
states?


Whatever their verdict. the vote
will put an end to the present
artificial boundary lines which the
conquering Allies imposed at the
end of the war.


Formerly Two States.


The three states involved are
Baden population 1.372.000)
Wuerttemberg-Bad population
1887, ,000) and Wuerttemberg-
Hohenzollern population 1894
000). They occupy the southwest
corner of Germany. along the
French and Swiss borders, and
have a combined population of
1893, 900.


Before the war, the area was
divided into two nearly equal
states, Baden and Wuerttemberg,
and the tiny province of Hohen-
zollern. The Allies carved the
area up into three states to fit
Occupation zone boundaries.
The Germans have complained
bitterly about this division ever
since. They have tried for years
to agree on merger. but the states
disagreed so sharply the federal
government had to intervene and
set up the plebiscite scheduled
for tomorrow.


Badenese Oppose Merger.
A previous poll showed that a
merger into one big southwest
state" is favored by about 80 per
cent of the areas residents except
In Baden.


Baden wants it's historic prewar
boundaries back again partly be-
cause of sentiment and partly
because the Badenese fear that
in a big state they would be the
poor relations" of the richer and
more aggressive Swabians of
Wuerttemberg.


About 100000 persons are ELI
gible to vote.

RICHMOND, Aug. IS. - Vir-
ginia's highway construction pro-
gram will be six months behind
schedule by the first quarter of
next year because Of the steel
shortage


And the situation will get pro-
gressively worse unless new high
way construction gets a larger
share of the country's steel pro-
duction.


This general review Of the sit
uation was confirmed today by
the State Highway Department.
The department put the blame
on two factors: .


l. ALLEGATIONS made by the Fed
eral Government for steel for new
road construction are too small.


Rubber Checks" Blamed.


2. The allocations, made quar-
terly. are released so late they
become rubber checks" and are
useless in actually obtaining steel
from producers.


The department. disclosed that
its top officials, including High
way Commissioner James A. An
derson, went to Washington last
week and laid their steel troubles
before Virginia's Congressional
delegation. So far, however, no
cure" has been announced, al
though advanced" ALLEGATIONS
are beginning to come through.


Steel for maintenance work, the
department said, is being obtained,
but estimated needs for new
projects are being cut so per cent
at the ALLEGATION stage.


For the third quarter Of this
year. the department reported, the
State agency's steel needs for new
projects were estimated at 1851
tons. The Federal Government
granted ALLEGATIONS amounting to
3,100 tons.


ALLEGATIONS Came Late.


The allocationS were not given
to the State until just about the
time the quarter began. When the
certificates were taken to the
mills, the department revealed,
the producers said their capacity
was already allocated and no de-
liveries to Virginia could be made.


Revalidation of the certificates
was necessary to get the steel
originally requested for the third
quarter in the fourth quarter. And
the department complained, these
Iorders were counted against the
States allotment for the fourth
quarter, 2.100 tons. -


Not counting the steel require
ments held over from the third
quarter, fourth quarter needs were
estimated at 4,548 tons.


The Department pointed out
Virginia was not alone in the
Federal wise on new road construc-
ton. All States were In the same
boat.


1t said defense production was
taking only 10 to IS percent of
the total steel output. whereas
road construction was being re-
quired to take a cut of so per
cent.

AUBURN. Ala. Feb. 26.-Au-
burn, starved for winning foot
ball team. reached over into
Georgia today and signed Ralph
Jordan, one of Wally Butts assist
ants, as head coach.


Whether Jordan can restore the
Tigers fortunes remains to be
seen. but Auburn viii give him
plenty Of time to try. under s.
year contract.


Jordan, 40 and a former Auburn
player, succeeds Earl M. Brown,
former Notre Dame star who was
fired two weeks ago under alumni
pressure after three losing seasons.


More than 100 coaches applied
for the job. but an alumni COM
mittee weeded the list down to
three and then two. The two top
candidates, Jordan and Norman
Cooper. Louisiana State line coach.
were presented to the faculty ath-
letic committee last night.


The committee interviewed them
and about three hours later the
committee went to President Ralph
B. Draughon with its recommen-
dation.





Draughon and Athletic Director
jeff Beard announced the selec-
ton early today. The salary was
not disclosed.


Jordan, who was line coach at
Georgia, was once an assistant
coach at Auburn. He is a native
of Selma. Ala, and is a veteran
of World War II. He was wounded
in the Normandy invasion.


Brown, formerly coach at Can
isius. won three games, tied four
and lost % during his three years
at Auburn.


Last year was the worst in the
schools history-Auburn lost every
game.


Gov. Gordon Persons, an ardent
alumnus. called for Browns dis
missal a few days after his inaug-
uration in January.
Auburn's last unbeaten football
team was in 1882.

ROME. Feb. 9.-New Commu-
mist defections blossomed in Italy
today as IA wartime partisan
chieftains lined up with Red rebels
against Moscow domination of the
party.


The group. all members Of the
Communicated Partisan Asso-
citation and all from the Red
stronghold of Reggie Emilia, de-
clared in a resolution that they
whole -heartedly supported Waldo
Magnani and Aldo Cucchi. who
quit the provincial party ranks
last week.


Believe in Defending Italy.


Magnani, who was Reggie
Enilian party secretary, and Cue
chi, holder of the Gold Medal,
Italy's highest award, left the fold
because they believed italian Com
munists should defend their coun-
try against all aggressors. includ-
ing Russia.


Fourteen partisan commanders,
including two who left the Com
munist Party Wednesday. called
the rebellion" of Magnani and
Cucchi a reaff1rmation =, Of the
"eminently patriotic character of
the (partisan) resistance"


Two mayors. another partisan
leader and Farpi Vignoli. a
prominent sculptor, also resigned
from the party yesterday.


Condemns Partisan Attack.

the Partisan Associations attack
on Magnani and Cucchi as evi-

Reports that Ignazio Silone,
ledaer of the anti-Communist
faction of the now badly split

Bologna to confer with Magnani
and Cucchi increased speculation
that they were trying to form a
new Communist party independ-
ent of Moscow.


Silone, an old friend of the two
ex-Communist leaders, is a we'll
known Italian author.

TOKYO, Sunday, Sept. 16.-The
Red China radio today charged
the United Nations with new viola
tions of the neutral zone at Kae-
song, site of the suspended Korean
armistice talks.


The Peiping broadcast quoted
a Communist correspondent in the
Korean truce talk city as reporting
the alleged violations occurred
within the past several days-since
the Allies admitted a single mis-
taken air violation September IL,
Alan Wilmington. correspondent
for the London Daily Worker, as
serted that South Korean troops
invaded this zone three times
and fired into it once" He said
they were dressed in American
uniforms.


Headquarters of Gen. Matthew
B. Ridgway, Allied supreme COM
mander, has emphatically denied
ali Red charges of neutral zone
violations except one-that an
Allied plane. through navigational
error, strafed the town last Mon
day in the dark.


The Allies Saturday put it
squarely up to the Communists
to take the next step toward re-
Stunning the truce talks.


| A statement issued by the public
information Office of Supreme
Allied Headquarters said "the next
move is now up to the Reds


The Reds broke off the talks
August %. They charged that
Allied warplanes strafed, bombed
and fire-bombed KaeSong the
night before in an attempt to
murder" the Communist truce
delegation. The United Nations
command denied it.


The statement Saturday dealt
primarily with another Commu-
mist charge-that an Allied air
craft bombed Kaesong last Mon
day. The United Nations admit
ted that charge, and said it was
the result of pilots mistake.


Reject "Trumped Up" Charges.


The statement said the admis-
sion was mo indication that the
United Nations command will ad-
NIT to any trumped-up Com
munist charge, no matter how
loudly they protest


"'The admission of the charge
puts the responsibility of the
"little cold war squarely up to the
Reds" the statement added.


The Reds have not yet officially
acknowledged the United Nations
note accepting blame for the Incl
dent.


The Allied release pointed out
that the straf1ng last Monday
occurred in a rather obscure area
a mile from the conference site
and was not-as the Reds have
falsely claimed before-aimed at
numbering the Red delegates"

The Civil Service Commission

same job in their agency.


The rehiring after their official
retirement" places them in the
category of temporary employees
who are eligible for social secur-
Iity benefits, since all Federal
workers hired during the national
emergency are given social secur-
lity coverage instead of civil serv-
ice retirement.


Consequently, Mr.. Ramspeck
said, these employees not only are
drawing full civil service retire

reach the age of IS they will also

Such dual pension coverage is

ment and social security systems, -
Mr.. Ramspeck declared.

end such practices Immediately.


Mr.. Ramspeck said that al

anxious that such practices be
avoided n the future.

touching Christmas party came to
pass last night for a large part OF
the city's blind.


A downtown department store
arranged an after-hours party in
its toyland for some $50 blind
children and their parents.


The sightless youngsters had as
gay time as luckier ones who can
see, riding the merry-go-round
and a toy jet plane. They whooped
madly, firing toy guns at imagi-
nary targets.


Little boys and girls carefully
ran their fingers over lines of
stuffed animals and other toys.
Like children everywhere, they
lined up-some bold, some anx-
ious, some shy-to tell Santa
Claus their Christmas wish.
headline:
Blind Detroit Youngsters
Are Guests Of Santa Claus

TACOMA. Wash. Dec. 8.-Tiny
Deborah Angelo kept up her un-
precedented struggle for life to-
day in a hospital air lock. -Four
days ago she was born with her
heart outside her body.


Skilled surgeons righted nature s
mistake shortly after her birth
Wednesday. The fact she still lives
makes medical history.


Doctors said there have been
only 88 recorded births with such
misplaced hearts. In only five
were corrective operations per-
formed. None of the infants sur
vived more than II hours.


The valiant little girl is the
daughter of Mr.. and Mrs. Elvor
Angelo Of nearby Puyallup. The
bed-confined mother got the Nrst
glimpse Of her daughter last night
"a picture after her surgery.

PARASITIC latest wrinkle In
European tourist travel is feet
Of 10 "drive-yourself" river boats.


Travellers now can rent a trim
little cabin cruiser by the day and
putt-putt up and down any one OF
half a dozen European rivers. ALI
inclusive rates: About $12 a day.


Organized by two retired British
naval officers. 1t. Comdr. Henry
Offord and Comdr D. w. (Tiger)
Child, the service offers a skipper
for each boat. More intrepid
travellers can run their own boat
If they think they can. An
SOS" call to service headquarters
will bring a trained sailor to tie
rescue in case of trouble.


Seldom Get Far.


Usually" says Comdr. Offord
with a chuckle, "the self-driverS
don't get very far before tele-
phoning our London Office for
help"


Right now, the partners main
venture is a fleet of five converted
wartime patrol boats-each carry
ing about 80 passengers on eight
and 15-day summer river cruises.
Rates range from 500 to $186, de-
pending on cabin accommodations
and length Of the cruise.


From last April through Sep
tember the yachts piled leisurely
courses through Hollands rivers,
lakes and canals and down the
Rhine and Main Rivers as far as
Frankfurt, Germany.


This year Comdrs. Offord and
Childs have scheduled nine 15-day
cruises up and down the Seine
River. their first invasion of
France. The trips start at Rouen,
near the seacoast. and follow the
winding Seine to Paris and Troyes,
some 300 miles inland. Shorter
week-long cruises also will be
made. A French chef does the
cooking.


The Seine River cruises are made
by the Master Standfast, which
early in the war ran the German
blockade Of Britain with vital ball
bearings from Sweden.


Child Is the Sailor.


Comdr. Offord, a 44-year-old
war veteran of Kensington, Lon
don, handles business and promo
ton. Comdr. Child, a much
decorated sea veteran of Deal,
England, runs the sailing side.
Comdr. Child, 46, lost leg in Hol-
land in 1910 and spent two years
in German prison camp before
being exchanged for a high
ranking friend of the Nazi bigwig,
Hermann Goering.


The partners began their cruise
business in 1886 but didn't really
get going until after the war. Then
they bought five speedy wartime
partol boats from the British
Admiralty, including three former
German craft, and converted them
into comfortable pleasure yachts.
War paint had to be scraped off
and guns demounted.


The Master Standfast, built with
a shallow draft to permit Passage
over mineflelds, can navigate
much farther upstream than other
craft of similar size. Cargo holds
have been converted into tidy
little one and two bed cabins.

made of the cost of producing
electric power from this reactor
with power from conventional
sources.

'hard-core' fanatics. Police had

Route II for the Catskills and

time and in some cases abandoned
their trips altogether.

lofflce-type paper supplies, turned
upside down across the four-lane
highway after a collision with an
automobile and spilled part of its
contents.

the accident scene, blocking other
trucks which were dispatched to
haul away the truck and it's con-
tents.

by police over a 13-mile detour

and from New York City and Up
state areas and the west were
delayed for hours.


State police said they never had
seen a worse tie-up.


Three persons were injured only
Slightly in the collision although
the automobile was almost de-
molished.

common sense has over aesthetics in the
long -drawn-out battle over repaving of the
bridge. Aesthetics had stalled for year the
use of $2o7 900 appropriation for repair of
the much Travelled span between the Lincoln
Memorial and Arlington. The delay resulted
from dispute between park and road officials

roadway-granite blocks. or asphalt. Asphalt

costly and less practical granite.

thing was done to reduce the shock on automo-
tive and human bodies. The situation pounded
along month after month"; until finally the
Fine Arts Commission was called in as arbiter.

practical considerations of safety and comfort
should prevail over any aesthetic considerations
involved in retaining the granite blocks. So
the rough surface soon is to be smoothed out
and overlaid with coating of nonartistic but
serviceable asphalt. Why 1t required year to
settle such simple pro1e remains mystery.

Office denied today that British
secret agents have located missing

said reports published in two Lon
don newspapers this morning were

The Foreign Office kept silent for
hours after the reports first ap-l

He said the search for the two

Daily EXpreSS-in other words,
Britain is still hunting for the two
officials.


Stories Quote Agents.


The newspaper stories quoted
agents of the British secret serv-
ice as saying they had located the
two diplomats who vanished with
out trace last May 25.


Mr.. Ridsdale said the agents
claimed they made no such state
ments. .....


He refused to say whether the
secret agents had made any state
mentS at all which might indicate

wide search for the two Britons
who were in position to know

the Foreign Office learned the
whereabouts of the two after
three month search by British
agents and Western European
police. 1t said MacLean had COM
municated with his American
born wife Melinda who is va
cationing with their three children

the governing Labor Party and has
close government connections.

in dispatch from Paris, said the
same story was current there and
added that Mrs. MacLean had left
her Riviera villa for a secluded ,
spot in the Var Mountains, so
miles away.
Neither story gave any hint
where the men supposedly are and
did not indicate one way or an
other whether they have disap-
peared behind the Iron Curtain.


The French police said Mrs.
MacLean told them she had no
idea Of where her husband is now,
and that she had received no mes
sage from her husband during her
vacation.


The two men have, been the
quarry in one of the greatest man
hunts of modern times since they
disappeared May 25. J.

American section of the Foreign
Office and Burgess, 40, had just

police over traffic violations.

government appeared concerned

diplomatic secrets. I.

CAIRO, Egypt, Dec. 10.-Egypt's S
government today considered sew
ering diplomatic relations with
Britain following leveling of an
Egyptian village by road-building
British soldiers.


Acting Foreign Minister Ibra-
him Farag Pasha said a decision
would be made soon. The cabinet
held two lengthy sessions yester-
day but a spokesman said only
that Anglo Egyptian relations
were discussed.


In the Suez Canal Zone the
British announced that two of
their soldiers were stabbed, beaten
and killed and a third was crit
ically wounded in Ismailia's Arab
quarter Saturday night.
An Egyptian communique re-
ported another Egyptian dead
from wounds received in the fight
ing at Suez last Tuesday, raising
to 81 the number of Egyptians
reported killed.


Clubs Lands COnfiscated.


The Egyptian cabinet yesterday
also approved a royal decree con-
f1Scating the lands of the 78-year-
old British-founded Gezira Sport
ing Club in Cairo, center of much
of the capitals social life.


The clubs 150-acre establish
ment includes a race course, polo
field and golf course, leased from
the government and situated in
Cairo'S most expensive foreign res
idential section.


Informants said that the cabi-
net also decided yesterday to dis
charges all Britons employed by
Egyptian government depart
mentS. The order repeatedly would
affect about $50 teachers, techni-
clans and other experts.


The proposal to sever diplomat
ic relations resulted directly from
British forces aggression in Suez, "
said the acting foreign minister
in referring to the demolition
Saturday of an Arab village out
side the city.


Demolition Not Resisted.


Heavily guarded British engi-
neers bulldozed down the Arab
huts with tanks to make way for
a new road and bridge.


Egyptian police had failed to
heed government orders to resist
the demolition. The new road,
linking the British garrison area
at SueZ with a water filtration
plant. bypasses a favorite spot for
Egyptian snipers. The British
said they completed it under the
protection of their troops yester-
day. without opposition.


A full severance of diplomatic
relations would mean the depar-
ture from Egypt of Britain's entire
diplomatic staff here, though con-
sular representation would con-
tinue. This would leave an
estimated 23,500 British civilians
in Alexandria, Cairo and the Suez
zone without the protection of
diplomatic representatives.

Break With Britain

McCLELLANVILLE, S. c., Nov
8.-Pure strain American wild
turkeys are making an assisted
comeback attempt in the Francis
Marion National Forest near here


The true American wild turkey
was almost extinct not too many
years ago. The forest area along
the lower reaches Of this states
muddy Santee River almost was
the only spot where the strain
still was found.


The South Carolina Game De-
partment is working under the
Federal Governments Pittman-
Robinson Game Management Law
toward development of what it
hopes will become an extensive
turkey trot" on $4,000 of the
forests 100000 acres.


Herman L. Holbrook, the pro-
ject manager. estimates there are
more than 600 turkeys in a IT,
000-acre tract cleared of live
stock and fenced against preda-
tory wild hogs.


When the project was started
In January, 1948, it was thought
there probably were no more than
$50 turkeys in the area. More
woodland is being cleared and
planted in grains, native grasses
and other turkey food.


The decline of the turkey popu-
lation dates from the time the
Coastal Plain pine forests began
to be cut. The big trees provided
just the right setting and didn't
permit much brush and hard
woods to grow.


AS the pines were cut out,
brush and hardwoods began to
encroach on the open spaces
where the turkeys normally find
their food.

Selective service officials have
told local draft boards that they
soon will receive details of the new
plan to allow draft liable college
students to enlist in the service of
their choice next summer.


The new policy. instigated by the
Defense Department. opens the
door for voluntary enlistments
even though the draft law says
men cannot VOLUNTEER after they
get orders for actual induction.


To bypass this provision. draft
officials plan to reopen the
draft classification status of STU
dents at the end of the school year,
even if they have been ordered for
induction.


Will Prevent Quitting.


The policy change was taken
to try to keep college students
from quitting school in mid term
in order to volunteer and beat
the draft.


Draft officials yesterday sent
Pentagon announcement of the
new policy to all draft boards,
a spokesman said. with word that
detailed instructions will follow
later.


Maryland draft officials, mean
while, instructed local draft
boards to sit tight on the new
defense policies.


Col. Asher Harman. State di-
rector, told draft boards to con-
tinue their current procedure of
ordering college students for
physicals and ordering them for
induction. Under the law. their
actual inductions are postponed
until the end of the academic
year.


End Seen Tuesday.


Col. Harman said the same ad-
vice held for students themselves.
They should take their physicals.
await induction calls and then re-
quest the postponements, he said.


Both House and Senate COM
mittees investigating the Penta-
CONS new universal draft plan for
l8-year- -olds were in recess until
Monday.


The Senate Preparedness Sub
committee hopes to wind up its
hearings Tuesday, then swing into
executive session to make specific
proposals on the draft expansion
plan.

ages three to fourteen, who were
home. all escaped without injury.

Buck Lodge, who owned the house
which burned. made another of

Fowlers.

been partially furnished from the
original stock of contributions
and more furniture donations
have been pledged.


More than six truck loads of
food, clothing, toys and furni-
ture were contributed in answer
to an appeal after the Fowler
tragedy, police said. Since that
is much more than the Fowlers
were able to use, police have been
distributing the surplus to about
dozen other needy families. in
cluding Mr.. and Mrs. Paal Dc"ne
and their three children. and Mr.
and Mrs. Howard Hunt and Their
baby, who were burned out Of
their home near Washington
Grove early Christmas Day.


Police said whatever is left
after the second distribution will
be turned over to welfare groups.
They said they are not accept
ing any further contributions ex-
cept money for the trust fund.

with its 20.059 students.

white school admitting a Negro
even at Federal Court insistence

funds.

JACKSON, Miss, Sept. 6.-Two
pro-Truman Democrats man
and his wife-pleaded guilty yes
terday to conspiring to sell Fed
eral jobs in Mississippi.


They were Mr.. and Mrs. C. v.
Murphy of Winona, Miss. Mrs.
Murphy was member of the pro-
Truman Mississippi Democratic
committee. Her husband was a
rural mail carrier until last April.


Federal Judge Allen Cox fined
Mrs. Murphy $3.50 and sentenced
her to eight months imprison-
ment, but said she would be placed
on probation if she paid the fine
in 10 days. She paid the fine.
Her husband was sentenced to
eight months Imprisonment.


Judge Cox then dismissed
charges of selling non-existent
Federal jobs, brought against Roy
Brashier and j. H. Wilkinson,
pro-Truman organizers. They
were charged with selling jobs as
county director of the Office of
Price Sterilization. The jobs did
not exist.


Mr.. Brashier and Mr.. Wilkin-
son are also charged with perjury
and with conspiracy to sell Fed
eral jobs.


Ten other persons connected
with the pro-Truman committee
attacked the constitutionality of
the law under which they were
indicted and the indictments
themselves.


Judge Cox gave defense attor-
neys 80 days to file any further
motions. He then recessed the
cases until January 8.

Two Plead Guilty
In Job Sales Case

Il am hopeful that we will be

Another attempt to save seven
Germans convicted of war crimes
from being hanged was made in
District Court yesterday.


Earlier habeas corpus actions
have failed. However, Attorney
Warren E. Magee. in two suits
filed yesterday, approached the
matter from new angles.


The suits ask for an interpreta-
ton of the United Nations Charter,
related treaties and executive
compacts. They were filed in be-
half of three generals, a colonel,
lieutenant-colonel, a sergeant
and an adjutant.


The suits contend that the state
of war between the United States
and Germany ended March 81,
when the United States recognized
the Federal Republic of Germany.
They declare that. when this
country recognized the German
republic. the Bonn Constitution
prohibiting capital punishment in
Germany became effective and
that, therefore, the seven Ger
mans may not be executed.


Those for whom the suits were
filed are Gen. Oswald Pohl, Brig.
Gen. Erich Naumann, Col. Paul
Blobel, 1t. Col. Werner Braune,
Maj. Gen. Otto Ohlendorf, Sergt.
George Schallermair and Adjutant
Hans Schmidt,

LONDON, May 3.-The Social
lists today voted an end to free
false teeth and eyeglasses for
Britons-but not before a lot OF
Laborites complained at length
about the new charges.


The House of Commons ap-
proved a bill to curtail the free
health services by a vote of 81
to 3. Opponents, who insisted on
being heard, prolonged debate
until early morning.


Many Laborites spoke in oppo-
sition to their party's measure
and a large bloc refrained from
voting. Most Conservatives-who
approve the new charge-also
abstained, although a handful
went along with the government.


The bill will require Britons to
pay half the cost of the spectacles
and dentures for the next three
years.


The Laborite leadership had
called for the cut in public health
costs to provide more money for
an expanded arms program.


This furnished the fuse for the
Labor Party rift that exploded
two weeks ago, when Health Min
lister Aneurin Bevan and two other
government members quit their
posts.


Mr.. Bevan and his adherents
contended that such a move vio-
lated the concept of free public
health service.


The bill set April, 1854, as the
time limit for charging for den
lures and spectacles unless Parli-
ament extends the deadline. The
time limit was a concession to
reluctant Laborites inclined to-
ward the Bevan view.

PARIS. Mar. 16.-The Nationa.
Assembly yesterday approved a
single ballot system of voting fol
the next French general elections


There has been growing senti-
ment among political leaders fol
holding elections June 3. Normal
ly they would be held in the fall
Completely reversing itself, the
National Assembly voted 318 to
282 for the single ballot system
under which the parties could
make coalitions. The Assembly
turned this down February %
leading to the resignation OF
Premier Rene Pleven.


The main object of changing the
election law from the old proper
tional representation system is to
cut the Communists down to size
The Communists have 1876 Depu-
ties. a larger number than any
other party.


Yesterdays vote was significant
in that the three government par
ties which supported the proposal
the Socialists, Catholic Popular
Republican Movement (MRP) and
moderate Radical Socialists-had
been split on whether to have a
single ballot or two votes a week
apart.

text:
G UMMER is the time for picnicking,
~ fishing and camping. It's also the
season for forest fires.


Thousands Of heat-jaded urbanites,
eager to escape the city on week ends
or during brief vacations, will travel this
summer to the forests and parks within
easy driving distance of the District of
Columbia. State and Federal foresters
welcome the use of forest recreational
areas. but they also realize that the dan
ger from fire rises sharply when thou
sands of people go to the woods.


Last year there were $500 forest fires
in the six States nearest the District
Virginia, Maryland, Delaware, West Vir-
ginia, Pennsylvania and New Jersey.
Each of these fires burned an average
of IA acres.


A 14-acre fire doesn't seem so bad, but
when all the burned forest areas in the
six States are added together they total
slightly more than $4,000 acres. Valu-
able timber was destroyed on those
$4,000 acres. But there were other in
direct losses, too. A forest fire hastens
erosion and increases flood danger. Fire
kills wildlife and blackens recreational
areas.


Only 18 of the $500 forest fires were
started by lightning. The remaining
6,591 fires were man-caused. All of
these man-caused fires could have been
avoided if people had been careful


Smokers must take the blame for
starting 1850 forest fires in the six
State area. They tossed lighted matches
or burning tobacco into dry forest litter
that smoldered while, then burst into
flames.


Debris burners ranked second with
1890 forest fires to their discredit.
These are the careless people who burn
leaves and trash on windy days or set
fire to brush piles in the woods. Before
they know it, the fire is out Of hand.


Sparks from trains started GIT fires
and campers caused 355 fires. If all
campers would follow the advice of
foresters-if they would see that camp
fires are entirely out before they leave
camp, these fires would never have
happened.


Offhand, the record of mans care
lessness in the forest looks pretty black.
headline: Time for Picnics- Forest Fires

leave Government employees should re-
ceive.


In this country. all Government en-
ployes are servants of the people, and
the people are the masters In all
master-servant relationships, the serv-
ants should not receive any greater
benefits than the masters.


Nowhere will you find private enter
prise giving employees over five weeks
q year paid vacation.


People employed in private enter
prise are paying taxes that give Govern
ment employees their salaries and vaca-
tions.


In simple justice to the people, who are
the masters; the servants, the Govern
ment employees, should have their leave
privileges cut down to at least the pre-
vailing practices in private enterprise.


Clifford L. Frank.
